note: Machine-readable factual provenance (Phase 9). Every spoken number in the story maps to a claim here. Distinct from media credits: this registry sources the CLAIMS the narration makes, not the images shown. The inline beats facts[] remain the human-readable summaries the description builder reads; this registry is what the facts gate enforces.

claims.claim: A typical U.S. worker earns about $2 million over a lifetime.
claims.source_title: Education and Lifetime Earnings / lifetime-earnings estimates
claims.publisher: U.S. Census Bureau; Social Security Administration
claims.calculation: Rounded from median lifetime earnings (~$1.7M nominal); higher with a bachelor's degree.
assumptions: Continuous full-time employment across the career
Rounded up to a $2M illustrative baseline
claims.uncertainty: Median vs mean and education level move this between ~$1.4M and ~$3M+.

claims.claim: Lifetime taxes total roughly $500,000 — about a quarter of earnings.
claims.source_title: Effective tax burden estimates (combined federal income, payroll, state, sales)
claims.publisher: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Tax Foundation
claims.calculation: ~25% average effective combined burden × the $2M lifetime baseline = $500k.
assumptions: Average effective (not marginal) rate held flat across the career
claims.uncertainty: State residency and income path move the effective burden roughly 18-32%.

claims.claim: Housing takes about a third of spending — roughly $500,000 over a lifetime.
claims.source_title: Consumer Expenditure Survey — housing ≈33% of average annual expenditures
claims.calculation: CES national-average housing share applied to lifetime income net of tax.
assumptions: National-average share; metro-area variation is large
Includes rent/mortgage, repairs, insurance, property tax
claims.uncertainty: High-cost metros exceed 40% of spending; low-cost regions run under 28%.

claims.claim: Getting around costs about a quarter of a million dollars over a lifetime.
claims.source_title: Consumer Expenditure Survey — transportation ≈16% of spending
claims.calculation: CES transportation share × lifetime post-tax spending; car payments, insurance, fuel, repairs.
assumptions: Car-dependent national average; transit-first households spend far less

claims.claim: Feeding yourself runs about $300,000 over a lifetime.
claims.source_title: Consumer Expenditure Survey — food at home + away ≈12-13% of spending
claims.calculation: CES food share (groceries + restaurants) × lifetime post-tax spending.
assumptions: Single-person share; family totals are higher per household but lower per person

claims.claim: Subscriptions and recurring fees siphon off about $150,000 over a lifetime.
claims.calculation: Survey-reported monthly subscription spend (~$200-270/mo incl. underestimation effect) × working-life months, rounded down conservatively.
assumptions: Survey self-reports systematically underestimate actual auto-renew spend
Streaming, memberships, and auto-renewing fees only — not utilities
claims.uncertainty: Survey-based; the point of the beat is order-of-magnitude, not precision.

claims.claim: About 15 cents of every dollar (~$300,000) remains as discretionary.
claims.source_title: Derived residual of the preceding claims
claims.population: the illustrative average worker of this story
assumptions: Pure arithmetic residual of the model's own figures
A teaching device, not a measured personal savings rate
claims.uncertainty: Inherits every upstream range; the narration frames it as the model's residual.
